query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A multi‐scale ab initio framework that explicitly couples electron–phonon interactions and anharmonic phonon scattering will decouple and accurately predict the separate lattice and electronic contributions to heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr, yielding at least a 20–30% improvement in predictive accuracy over traditional Debye-temperature–based models.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr in its ideal, defect‐free crystalline state and a variant with ~1 wt.% oxygen contamination.
generation.intervention: Application of an advanced multi‐scale ab initio simulation method that simultaneously computes electron–phonon coupling and anharmonic lattice vibrations.
generation.conditions: Valid across low temperatures (<200 K) where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable, and mid- to high-temperatures (300–1200 K) as evidenced by experimental total conductivity measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Explicitly calculated electronic band structure and phonon dispersion (including anharmonic effects) that mediate electron transport and lattice heat conduction respectively.
generation.mechanism: By dynamically coupling the electron and phonon subsystems, the method decouples the contributions: electron–phonon interactions determine electronic conductivity while anharmonic phonon scattering controls lattice conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The new approach will yield separate, quantitatively accurate predictions for lattice and electronic thermal conductivities. In the low-temperature regime, the predicted values should mirror the experimental comparability of both contributions, while at high temperatures the sum should approximate the observed total conductivity (~10–17 W/(K m)).
generation.baseline: Earlier approaches based on variations in atomic mass, force constants, and Debye temperature estimates which assumed perfect, defect-free crystalline behavior.
generation.boundary: The method is expected to be valid for crystalline HfNbTaTiZr with minimal oxygen contamination; its accuracy may diminish for alloys with high levels of extrinsic defects or amorphization.
generation.uncertainty: The estimated 20–30% improvement in prediction accuracy is based on preliminary simulations; uncertainties remain regarding precise error bounds when incorporating real-world complexities such as oxygen impurities.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a set of controlled experiments to separately measure the lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity in both pure and ~1 wt.% oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr specimens over the temperature ranges <200 K and 300–1200 K, and compare these results with predictions from the new ab initio framework.
measurements: Direct measurement of lattice thermal conductivity using techniques that suppress electronic transport (e.g., by applying high magnetic fields or through isotope substitution).
Independent measurement of electronic conductivity through electrical resistivity (using the Wiedemann–Franz relation adjusted for low temperature deviations).
Total thermal conductivity across the temperature range using steady-state or transient techniques.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the decoupled predictions for lattice and electronic thermal conductivities deviate by more than approximately 20–30% from the experimental measurements across the specified temperature regimes, or if the framework fails to capture the comparative balance of contributions (<200 K) and the overall total conductivity (300–1200 K).

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) provide new research avenues for alloy combinations in the periodic table, opening numerous possibilities in novel-alloy applications. However, their electrical characteristics have been relatively underexplored. The challenge in establishing an HEA electrical conductivity model lies in the changes in electronic characteristics caused by lattice distortion and complexity of nanostructures. Here we show a low-frequency electrical conductivity model for the Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEA system. The cocktail effect is found to explain trends in electrical-conductivity changes in HEAs, while the magnitude of the reduction is understood by the calculated plasma frequency, free electron density, and measured relaxation time by terahertz spectroscopy. As a result, the refractory HEA Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 thin film exhibits both high hardness and excellent conductivity. This combination of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 makes it suitable for applications in atomic force microscopy probe coating, significantly improving their wear resistance and atomic-scale image resolution. In this work, we present a framework to explore Pareto-optimal compositions by integrating advanced ab initio-based techniques into a Bayesian multi-objective optimization workflow, complemented by a simple analytical model providing straightforward analysis of trends. The term “high-entropy alloy” was introduced by Yeh et al. in 2004 [,]. The multiple principal elements in HEAs, especially those with significant atomic radius differences, cause lattice distortion []. The lattice distortion and inherent chemical disorder of HEAs lead to fluctuations in interatomic force constants and mass, resulting in intensified anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions [] and a reduced lattice thermal conductivity. Studies have shown that HEAs exhibit semimetallic characteristics, where the contribution of phonons to heat conduction can be comparable to that of electrons []. Moreover, charge carriers can move freely when the phonons are hindered and scattered, which is beneficial for achieving a high ZT (thermoelectric figure of merit) value as well as a high efficiency in thermal-energy management []. These features suggest that HEAs are potential next-generation thermoelectric materials. Therefore, researching the thermal physical properties and heat transfer mechanisms of HEAs is of great significance.
